sources.name: Clara Dallaire-Fortier — MinCan, March 2024
sources.description: 947 Canadian principal mine records with production phases and coordinates. This adaptation selects supported non-fossil primary commodities, preserves reopening/suspension phases, bounds open mines to 2022 and excludes explicitly museum-based coordinates. Co-products without dated extraction evidence are not projected across a mine’s lifetime.

sources.name: Jasansky, Lieber, Giljum & Maus — Global coal and metal mine production, version 1.0.3
sources.description: Published global mine evidence linked to company reports; non-fossil production observations in this release end in 2020. This adaptation selects mines with published coordinates and uses production-start/end bounds plus positive ore or commodity output at those mining facilities. The source may estimate production from processing/sales proxies; marked quantity estimates are identified, and known stockpile-only years and shutdowns remain excluded. Canadian mines use MinCan; global iron mines use GIOMT; West African gold is reviewed separately.

sources.name: Global Energy Monitor — Global Iron Ore Mines Tracker, September 2026
sources.license: Tracker data: CC BY 4.0; factual dates from separately cited GEM wiki revisions (original wiki text: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
sources.description: September 2026 public map, enriched with factual production start/stop dates and observations from individually versioned factsheets. No wiki prose is redistributed. Lifetime intervals are approximate and may contain undocumented shutdowns; no planned/future start or closure is used.

mincan.information: Alternative names: Horne Mine (1975) The mine is named after prospector Edmund Horne who first staked the property in 1920. The property was optioned in 1922 to a syndicate that discovered a major copper-gold deposit and grew to become Noranda Mines Limited, later Noranda Inc., one of the world's premier mining and metals companies. The deposit in Precambrian Keewatin-type volcanic rocks is a classic example of a volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS) deposit. The Horne mine exploited two major ore bodies called the Upper H and the Lower H. The ore averaged 2.22% Cu, 6.1 g/t Au and 13 g/t Ag. The mine closed in 1976,having produced 53.7 million tons of ore and recovering 260t of gold (11.6 million ounces) and 1.13Mt of copper. The Horne copper smelter built on the mine site in 1927 is still in operation. Mineral rights are currently (2015) owned by Falco Resources Ltd which is examining the feasibility of mining the Horne 5 copper-gold deposit below the old Horne mine workings.

The mine was also in operation from 1928 to 1939.

From 1953 to 1955, Makeno Mines Ltd produced 57,856 tonnes of ore. From 1956 to 1957, Galkeno Mines Ltd produced 47,015 tonnes and from 1959 to 1966, and again from 1978 to 1980, United Keno Hill Mines Ltd produced  26,382 tonnes of ore. Total production from the mine was 167,063 tonnes at a grade of 932.57 g/t silver (27.2 oz/t), 5.22% lead and 2.69% zinc to produce 141,338,613 grams of silver (4,544,142 oz), 7,909,476 kg of lead, 8,999,204 kg of zinc and 39,146 kg of cadmium. ////// closed between 2019 and 2020

Even more companies : Barrick Gold, Cambior, ...The Doyon site was the subject of more intense prospecting in the 1960’s by the prospector Arthur Doyon. In 1972, it became the co-property of Silverstack Mines Company Ltd and of SOQUEM, which carried out exploration works between 1972 and 1975. In 1977, Long Lac Mineral Exploration Ltd (Lac Minerals Ltd) took over Silverstack Mines Ltd, and a drilling survey of 120 holes brought the Doyon deposit into production in February 1980. In 1983, a surface exploration campaign led to the discovery of Doyon West Zones.
The Cadillac-Bousquet region in northwestern Québec has been a productive mining centre for over 100 years and still holds great potential. In 1972, it became the co-property of Silverstack Mines Company Ltd. and the Québec government controlled Soquem Inc., which carried out exploration between 1972 and 1975. In 1975 Long Lac Mineral Exploration Ltd (Lac Minerals Ltd), took over Silverstack’s interest. Commercial open pit mining began at the Doyon Mine in 1980, and while underground mining commenced in 1985, the full transition to a wholly underground operation was completed in early 1989. The Doyon Gold Mine has been a significant producer of gold for the past 30 years having produced over 5 million ounces of gold.
 
In 1986, Cambior Inc. acquired an initial 50% interest in the Doyon Gold Mine and 100% of the Mouska property in connection with the privatisation of most of Soquem’s assets. Cambior became the sole owner of the Doyon Gold Mine by acquiring the remaining 50% interest from Barrick Gold in 1998.

The Nipissing Mine is an abandoned silver mine in Cobalt, Ontario, Canada, located on Nip Hill on the east side of Long Lake.[1]

It was developed in the subsequent Cobalt silver rush of 1903.[2] The original 843 acres of claims were purchased by Ellis P. Earle from the Ferland Syndicate. By 1907, it was the top producing mine in the area. The company completely surrounded Peterson and Carr lakes and occupied the east side of Cobalt Lake. At its peak, the mine had ten shafts working three veins, the Kendall, Meyer and Fourth of July. Additionally, it used hydraulics to strip the overburden and employed an aerial tramway. The last dividend was paid in 1921 however. The mine continued to operate during the 1920s by harvesting remnants and areas overlooked during the early boom years. With the onset of the Great Depression, the price of silver collapsed and the mine became uneconomic. Underground exploration and rock breaking had ceased by 1932 and further production was from various rock dumps. In 1952 the company merged with O'Brien Mines to become Nipissing-O'Brien Mines with minor operations through extraction of floors and pillars in the old workings. The resultant company would later merge into Agnico Mines which was a forerunner to Agnico-Eagle Mines of today

Puis, il fut donné au bureau de poste et, ensuite, retenu par Joseph Bradley pour désigner l’usine de fabrication de peinture dont les bâtiments étaient de couleur rouge, tout comme l’ocre, de laquelle on tirait les pigments utilisés dans la fabrication de la peinture. Au cours des décennies 1870, 1880 et 1890, pas moins de quatre entrepreneurs et entreprises s’aventurèrent, sans trop de succès, à exploiter le gisement de Red Mill: Télesphore-Eusèbe Normand (1887), la Johnson Magnetic Iron Paint Company (1888), James Robertson (1888-1892) et la Saint-Maurice Metallic Paint Company (1891-1893). Mais, après s’être assuré les services de John Bradley, un Anglais de Derby passé maître dans l’art de préparer des pigments, le fabricant de peinture Canada Paint ouvrit une usine de traitement et de transformation à Red Mill en 1892. Durant les deux premières années de ses activités, la Canada Paint réussit à produire 31 couleurs pour l’industrie de la peinture. Jusqu’en 1911, elle produisit en moyenne 950 tonnes de minerai par année. En 1922, l’usine et la mine de Canada Paint à Red Mill furent acquises par la Sherwin-Williams Corporation of Canada Limited. Les «terres à peinture» apportèrent du pain sur la table de la plupart des familles du rang Saint-Malo. L’épuisement des gisements d’ocre, durant les années 1950, entraîna la fermeture de tous les établissements spécialisés dans la vente d’oxyde de fer. L’entreprise Sherwin-Williams de Red Mill ferma ses portes en 1966. James Bradley et ses associés formèrent aussitôt la compagnie Red Mill Industries Limitée et tentèrent de relancer l’usine en décembre de la même année. Mais l’usine ferma définitivement ses portes en 1968, après 75 ans d’activité.

reconciliations.reason: Same named Scully mine and coherent positions. Operator reports supersede the coarse MinCan dates and preserve the 2014–2019 shutdown; a single GEM lifetime span must not fill it.

periods.description: Operator technical report, history section: commercial mine operated from 1965 until February 2014. Construction and pilot-plant years are excluded.

Operator records the May 2019 restart of mining. Continued operation is attested by the September 2026 GEM tracker snapshot; 2026 is an evidence endpoint, not a closure date. The earlier shutdown is preserved.

reconciliations.reason: Same Bloom Lake mine. The operator's historical production table corrects the inverted/incomplete MinCan phases, preserving 2015–2017 non-production.

periods.description: Champion Iron 2023 Annual Information Form, Table 6-1: historical mine production from 2010–2014, with no production in 2015–2017.
Operator documents the February 2018 restart. Operation remains attested in the September 2026 GEM snapshot; the 2015–2017 gap is not bridged.

reconciliations.reason: Same Fire Lake mine, both sources at the same site. Operator history and Quebec ministry chronology establish a first extraction in 1977 and reopening in 2006; preserve the intervening closure.

periods.description: Operator report states first extraction in 1977; MinCan records the end of the original phase in 1984. The earlier source opening date is not treated as extraction.
Quebec ministry chronology records reopening in 2006; the September 2026 GEM snapshot attests operating status. Seasonal interruptions may occur within annual operation years.

reconciliations.reason: Mont-Wright and Fire Lake are separate mines about 53 km apart in the operator's report. GEM's Mont-Wright coordinate nearly duplicates Fire Lake; use the independently published MinCan Mont-Wright coordinate, preserving correct identity.

periods.description: Operator property history and MinCan attest operation from 1976; current operation is attested by the September 2026 GEM snapshot. The endpoint does not imply a closure.

reconciliations.reason: Same Mary River mine. MinCan repeats latitude as the absolute longitude (-71.340446,71.340446), hundreds of kilometres from the actual mine. The GEM position and production-start evidence are preferred; the erroneous MinCan record is excluded.
MinCan Wesfrob (Tasu) and Wesfrob Mining Division share the unique name, primary iron, exactly the same 1914–1983 production phase and positions less than 1 km apart. Retain one record.

Marmoraton mine and Marmoraton Mining Co. near Marmora identify the same iron operation within 400 m. Keep the conservative later production phase (1955–1978), rather than the ambiguous 1948 opening date.
Identical Silvertip name and coordinates. Coeur annual reports supersede contradictory MinCan phases and preserve the February 2020 suspension; no reopening is inferred.

periods.description: Coeur reports commercial production from September 2018 and suspension of mining and processing in February 2020. Earlier development and later proposed restarts are excluded.

reconciliations.reason: Identical Seleine name and coordinates. Windsor Salt and Quebec government records establish first operation in 1982, rather than the earlier development dates in MinCan.

periods.description: Windsor Salt confirms operation since 1982; the 2022 Quebec environmental decision attests continued extraction and shipment operations. 2022 is the latest consulted attestation, not a closure date.

reconciliations.reason: Identical Boss Mountain coordinates, unique mine name, molybdenum commodity and production phase 1965–1983. Company-labelled duplicate removed.
Same Saskatoon Chemicals salt operation at identical coordinates, with old and subsequent company-labelled records; preserve both attested phases as one site.

periods.description: First of two consecutively recorded MinCan phases for the same Saskatoon Chemicals operation.
Subsequent MinCan phase under the Weyerhaeuser-labelled company record; open as of the 2022 evidence snapshot.

reconciliations.reason: Both named Heath Steele records identify the same zinc mine within 0.45 km. The provincial geological guide and operator technical report replace contradictory MinCan lifetime dates, exclude stockpile treatment following 1983, and discard the unsupported 2007–2008 reopening. Mid-year suspensions retain their partly productive boundary years at annual resolution.

periods.description: New Brunswick geological guide documents mining from 1957 until the 1958 suspension; the earlier MinCan development date is excluded.
Provincial guide documents renewed extraction from 1962 until the 1983 shutdown. Later treatment of previously stockpiled gossan does not establish new extraction.
Mining resumed in 1989 and was suspended in mid-1993. The partly productive year 1993 remains visible; the ensuing suspension is documented separately.

Provincial guide records resumption in mid-1994; the operator technical report confirms final cessation in October 1999. The separate preceding phase preserves the mid-1993 to mid-1994 interruption in provenance, although annual map resolution cannot display the partial-year gap.

reconciliations.reason: Same Birchtree nickel mine, 0.17 km apart. Manitoba production history supersedes inconsistent MinCan development/opening dates and confirms the 1977–1989 suspension; Vale reports the September 2017 care-and-maintenance decision.

periods.description: Manitoba mineral inventory documents first production in 1969 and suspension in December 1977; earlier shaft/development dates are not extraction dates.

Manitoba government chronology records production resumption in 1989. Vale September 2017 production report confirms placement on care and maintenance at the end of that month; no later resumption is inferred.

reconciliations.reason: The two Canadian Malartic records represent the old underground mine and the reworked deposit now exploited by the modern open pit, about 2.97 km apart within the mining complex. Preserve the original mine history under the stable modern ID without bridging 1966–2010.

periods.description: Canadian Malartic operator report distinguishes discovery in 1926 from underground exploitation in 1935, followed by closure in 1965. Other Malartic district mines operated on different dates and are not substituted for this mine.

Operator history confirms commercial mining from May 2011; MinCan attests the operation as open in 2022. That evidence endpoint is not a closure date. Earlier exploration and construction are excluded.

reconciliations.reason: The two named Detour Lake gold records are 0.27 km apart. Canada Gazette confirms original extraction from 1983 to 1999 and a January 2013 production restart, correcting the continuous 1983–2022 MinCan row.

periods.description: Canada Gazette records open-pit and underground mining between 1983 and 1999. The 2000–2012 closure is preserved.
Canada Gazette confirms production restarted in January 2013; MinCan records the mine as operating in 2022. No operation during the preceding closure or beyond this evidence endpoint is inferred.

reconciliations.reason: Same Cochenour-Willans/Cochenour gold mine within 0.09 km. Museum history and Ontario mineral inventory establish production from 1939, not the 1932 surface-development date. Historic and recent phases remain separate. The museum describes a wartime suspension in 1944; 1945 is conservatively left unassigned because fiscal production totals straddle calendar years and the restart date is not precise.

periods.description: Museum history dates first production to 1939 and a wartime suspension to 1944. The partly productive suspension year is retained; earlier exploration and shaft construction are excluded.

Ontario inventory contains positive annual production records from 1946 onward and explicitly dates cessation of mining to August 1971. The museum describes a post-war restart without a precise date: 1946 is the first retained reporting year, not an asserted reopening date; 1945 remains a documentary gap. Closure/flooding in 1975 is not treated as extraction.
Separate modern Cochenour production phase recorded by MinCan, open as of its 2022 snapshot. Exploration/dewatering between the old and new operations does not fill the long extraction gap.

rules.coordinates: Published mine coordinates only; invalid and explicit museum positions excluded. Multipoint complexes use a published actual point, never a country/municipality centroid.
rules.temporal: Finite production-phase bounds or dated extraction observations; no discovery/construction dates or inferred future operation. Approximate lifetime periods are explicitly labelled.
rules.exclusions: Undated deposits, non-mining industrial facilities, unsupported commodities, Canadian FINEPRINT duplicates, West African gold under separate review.
